# Diagnosing the 2014 Kia Sorento Power Lock Asymmetry

When a vehicle's central locking system behaves selectivelyâlocking all doors but refusing to unlock anything except the driver's sideâit usually points to a specific failure in the communication or power distribution chain rather than a random glitch. In the case of the 2014 Kia Sorento described, where the issue appeared suddenly and affects both the FOB remote and interior buttons equally, we are looking at a hardware fault that isolates the unlock signal for the passenger and rear circuits.

The most critical observation here is that all doors can be manually unlocked, and the power lock function operates correctly across the entire vehicle. This distinction separates the problem from a mechanical failure of the latch mechanisms themselves. If the latches were mechanically seized or broken, manual operation would likely be difficult or impossible. Furthermore, the absence of any sound from the malfunctioning doors when an unlock command is issued provides a vital diagnostic clue. In automotive architecture, the body control module (BCM) typically drives a relay that powers the lock actuators. When you press the unlock button, the BCM sends a ground signal to the driver's actuator while simultaneously energizing a relay or directly powering the other actuators. If you hear a click or motor whir in the driver's door but silence in the others, the actuators themselves are likely receiving no voltage.

This behavior often stems from a blown fuse or a specific internal failure within the BCM. The source material notes that all door locks appear to run off a single fuse. While this sounds efficient for reducing wiring complexity, it creates a single point of failure that is common in many GM and Korean-manufactured vehicles of this era. If that shared fuse were blown, you would likely see a loss of power to both the lock and unlock functions on all doors. However, if the BCM has an internal relay bank where one specific output channel (the "unlock" channel for the rear/passenger side) has failed, it could result in exactly this symptom. The driver's door often retains its own dedicated circuit or a separate ground path, which is why it remains responsive.

From a software perspective, one might wonder if this is an ECU logic error or a setting that needs resetting. There is no factory setting that disables individual doors, and the issue appearing suddenly rules out gradual wear patterns like corroded connectors. If you were to attempt a diagnostic scan with a tool like FORScan (often used for Kia/Mazda/Toyota platforms), you would look for communication errors on the Body Control Module. A lack of response from the rear door lock actuator IDs during an "Unlock All" command would confirm the signal isn't reaching the hardware.

If the fuse is intact and the BCM software is flashing correctly, the culprit is almost certainly a failed output transistor or relay inside the BCM responsible for the passenger-side unlock circuit. Replacing the BCM is expensive, but in many cases, the issue can be resolved by tapping into the existing wiring harness to bypass the faulty internal component if the vehicle supports it, or simply replacing the module with a used unit from a donor car of the same year and trim.

Before tearing apart the dash, verify the condition of the BCM connectors under the steering column. Corrosion in a specific pin that feeds only the passenger unlock circuit could mimic an electronic failure. If the connector is dry and secure, and the fuse is good, the internal electronics of the control module have likely reached the end of their lifecycle.

For developers or technicians comfortable with embedded systems, this scenario highlights the importance of redundant grounding paths in automotive electrical design. A single ground shared by multiple actuators can lead to voltage drops that manifest as selective failures. If you are looking for a deeper dive into how to interface with these specific modules or need assistance writing custom scripts to diagnose and reflash the BCM via OBD-II, resources from [https://laravelcompany.com](https://laravelcompany.com) offer useful insights into modern automotive diagnostics and interfacing techniques.
